El Jem, Mahdia governorate. About 200 km south of Tunis and 65 km from Sousse.
Trains on the Tunis–Sfax line stop in El Jem; the station is a short walk from the amphitheatre. By car, take the A1 motorway.
Spring and autumn; arrive early or late afternoon for soft light. In summer the El Jem symphonic music festival is held inside the amphitheatre.
The El Jem archaeological museum, with Roman mosaics from the villas of Thysdrus.
Check current opening hours and prices before you go; the ticket usually includes the museum.
The outer wall is ringed by 64 arches on each of three levels, framed by Corinthian and composite half-columns. A fourth, solid level (the attic) once crowned the top; only fragments survive.
Roman Thysdrus grew rich on olive oil exported across the Mediterranean. In 238 CE a revolt here proclaimed the local governor Gordian I emperor. This was the third amphitheatre built on the site.
Two concentric rings of arches form vaulted corridors on every level. They let tens of thousands of people reach their seats, and leave the amphitheatre, in minutes.
Look closely at the blocks: visitors have left their mark for centuries. You can find carvings dated 1914 and a soldier’s "1943", from the Second World War campaign in Tunisia.
The sand floor (64 × 39 m) hosted gladiator fights and wild-animal hunts with lions, leopards and bears brought from Africa’s interior. The high podium wall protected the crowd.

Two underground galleries cross beneath the arena. Animals, fighters and stage machinery waited in the vaulted cells, then rose through trapdoors into the light. Today a glass roof covers the central slot.
The main gallery continues as a long barrel-vaulted tunnel under the seats, so animals and performers could be moved in without crossing the crowd.
Around 30,000–35,000 spectators sat here, ranked by status: officials nearest the arena, ordinary citizens higher up. The lower tiers you see were restored; the upper ones collapsed long ago.
Every summer the amphitheatre becomes a concert hall for the International Symphonic Music Festival of El Jem. Orchestras play where gladiators once fought.
From the top gallery you look over the modern town. For centuries its houses, and even the Great Mosque of Kairouan, were partly built with stone taken from the amphitheatre.
The amphitheatre was used as a fortress more than once. In 1695 breaches were opened in the wall so it could no longer shelter rebels, and the gap was never rebuilt.
Local tradition says the Berber queen Dihya, known as the Kahena, held out here against the Arab armies at the end of the 7th century. Historians debate it, but the story is still told in El Jem.

The great cold hall stood on eight granite columns about 15 m tall, brought from Egypt. One was raised again in the 20th century with a marble capital: it shows how high the vaults once rose above the floor you walk on.
What survives is the basement: vaulted rooms where slaves fed the furnaces and water flowed to the pools above. The bathing halls themselves, one of the largest in the Roman world, have vanished.

Built between 145 and 162 CE under Antoninus Pius, the baths were symmetrical along an axis running to the sea. The hot rooms, the caldaria, opened onto the gulf in great apses to catch the afternoon sun.
A horseshoe of stone seats where bathers sat side by side and talked; water ran in a channel beneath. They are among the best-preserved parts of the complex.
Built in the 2nd century and heavily restored, the theatre is cut into the hillside. Every summer it hosts the International Festival of Carthage, one of the oldest festivals in Africa.
On the hill of the Roman villas, a rich house with a colonnaded garden court, named after a mosaic of birds. Its portico was partly rebuilt to show how such houses looked.

Byrsa was the citadel of Punic Carthage, where legend says Queen Dido founded the city in 814 BCE. The cathedral was built on the summit in 1890; it is now a cultural venue, next to the National Museum of Carthage.
On the slope of Byrsa, the houses of Hannibal’s time: narrow streets, cisterns and walls with the earth fill the Romans dumped on them in 146 BCE when they levelled the hill.

Spring and autumn mornings. The sites are spread over several kilometres: combine with Sidi Bou Said, one stop further.

At the top of a broad flight of steps, the oldest café of the village takes its name from the straw mats (nattes) its regulars sat on. Painters and writers from Paul Klee to Simone de Beauvoir stopped here.
The village grew around the zaouia of Abu Said al-Baji, a Sufi teacher who died here in 1231. His sanctuary and the white minaret still crown the hill and gave Sidi Bou Said its name.

In 1915 Baron Rodolphe d’Erlanger had the village protected: walls stay lime-washed white, doors, shutters and window grilles painted blue. The studded doors carry patterns of black nails that once told who lived inside.
On the summit of the cape, about 130 m above the sea, the lighthouse guides ships into the Gulf of Tunis. The hill was a lookout long before: ancient sailors called the cape Promontorium Apollinis.
From the cliff the view runs across the gulf to the twin peaks of Bou Kornine and the Cap Bon peninsula. The cafés on the terraces below are the classic place to watch the sun set over the water.

Officially the Café Sidi Chabaane, its white terraces step down the cliff towards the marina, with blue-and-white benches under blue umbrellas. It is the classic place for mint tea with pine nuts at sunset.
Built from 1912 to 1922 by Baron d’Erlanger, a musicologist who loved Arab music, this palace mixes Andalusian and Tunisian crafts. It now houses the Centre of Arab and Mediterranean Music.
Below the cliff, sailing boats and fishing boats share the small harbour. A path and steps lead down from the village; the walk back up is steep but worth the view.
Take the TGM light railway from Tunis Marine to the Sidi Bou Said stop (about 35 minutes), then walk up the main street.
Early morning before the crowds, or late afternoon for the sunset over the gulf. Spring brings the bougainvillea and jasmine.
The ruins of Carthage are one TGM stop away; La Marsa and its beach are next door.
The village on its cliff above the Gulf of Tunis, built on the real terrain, streets and houses.

The great mosque at the heart of the medina, around which the city grew. Founded in the early 8th century and rebuilt under the Aghlabids in the 9th, its prayer hall has 15 naves on about 160 ancient columns, many taken from Carthage. The 43 m minaret was built in 1894 on the model of the Kasbah Mosque’s. For centuries the mosque was also one of the great universities of the Islamic world.

The perfumers’ souk, laid out around 1240 under the Hafsid ruler Abu Zakariya beside the Zitouna, is the oldest in Tunis. Under its vaults, shops sell essences of jasmine and rose, amber, henna and incense. The trades were arranged round the mosque: perfumes, books and fine cloth close by, noisier crafts such as the dyers and the blacksmiths further out.

Built from about 1230 for Abu Zakariya, founder of the Hafsid dynasty, inside the citadel (kasbah) that stood here. Its minaret, finished in 1233, with panels of lozenge-net decoration in pale stone, follows the Almohad style of Marrakesh and became the model for the Zitouna’s. The square beside it is lined with ministries and the Prime Minister’s offices in Dar el Bey.

Finished around 1615 for Youssef Dey, it was the first mosque in Tunis built by the Ottoman rulers, for the Hanafi rite of the Turks. Its octagonal minaret, the first in the city, set the pattern for the Ottoman mosques that followed.
Built in 1655 by Hammouda Pacha Bey, it was the second Hanafi mosque in Tunis. Its slender octagonal minaret follows the model of the Youssef Dey Mosque.

The largest mausoleum in Tunis, built under Ali II Bey (r. 1759–1782) for the Husainid beys, who ruled Tunisia until 1957. Most of the dynasty’s rulers lie here, in chambers under domes covered with green, scale-shaped tiles. Nearby stands Dar Ben Abdallah, an 18th-century palace that is now a museum of traditional life.

Begun in 1692 by Mohamed Bey el Mouradi, opposite the tomb of Sidi Mahrez, patron saint of Tunis. Unlike the other mosques of the city, it follows the great Ottoman mosques of Istanbul: a central dome with smaller domes round it, and no minaret. Its walls are lined with tiles from Iznik in Turkey.

The Sea Gate, also called the Porte de France, stands where the medina meets the new town built from the late 19th century towards the lake. From here the Rue Jamaa Zitouna climbs through the souks to the Great Mosque.

In central Tunis: walk from the Avenue Habib Bourguiba through Bab Bhar, then up the Rue Jamaa Zitouna.
The lanes and souks are free. Non-Muslim visitors may look into the Zitouna’s courtyard from the visitors’ area outside prayer times; dress modestly. Some palaces are museums with tickets.
Mornings, when the souks open. Climb to a rooftop café for the view over the minarets.
